## Performance test
### usage

As a means to replace the Array referenced in the return value of a ClassMethodPtrCall. ie an exposed getter method.


### methodology
run for 1000 frames. In each frame call a series of GDE methods (same method(s) repeated 25 times) in order to dereference and assign an array to an initialized TypePtr. Begin a stopwatch before the GDE methods were called, stop it after they are completely called. Assign the time in nanoseconds to an array.

Two methods were used
1. call array_ref
2. call Destroy followed by the Create1 copy constructor

Stopwatch has100 nanosecond precision. sub 100 it would report 0
time is reported in nanoseconds

using Godot release version 4.6
OS Windows 11
language Odin
compiled with -o:speed
launch via cli C:\\Godot\\Godot_v4.6-release.exe --path ./TopDown

### code
```
//Called each frame through a getter from GDScript
get_tPtr_Array_passthrough :: proc "c" (method_userdata: rawptr, p_instance: GDE.ClassInstancePtr, args: [^]rawptr, r_return: ^Array) {
    ret: Array
    get_passthrough(method_userdata, p_instance, args, &ret)
    watch: time.Stopwatch
    if counter < 1000 {
        time.stopwatch_start(&watch)
        //One of the two below repeated 25 times
        gdAPI.Packed_Array_Utils.ArrayRef(r_return, &ret)
        //Destroy(r_return)
        //GDW.Array_M_List.Create1(r_return, {&ret})
        time.stopwatch_stop(&watch)
        _, _, s, nano:= time.precise_clock(watch)
        times_baseline[counter]=nano
        if nano > slowest do slowest = nano
        if nano < fastest do fastest = nano
        counter+=1
    } else {
        if timer_once == false {
            context = runtime.default_context()
            fmt.println(times_baseline)
            k:int
            for i in times_baseline {
                k+=i
            }
            fmt.println("average", k/1000)
            fmt.println("slowest", slowest)
            fmt.println("fastest", fastest)
            timer_once = true
        }
    }
```

### short conclusion

This is a very rudimentary test which only looks at one use case. This does not look at a case where the source or destination is a null value. There are several checks to exit earlier from the = operator overload for those.

On average array_ref is more than 2x faster. Taking the fastest times the difference is 4-6x.
I'm not sure where the outliers are coming from, could be due to the ref counting itself?

If there is no other direct equivalent via GDE interface I will be using array_ref for at least this use case.

There are several problems with your measurement:

>    ```odin
>        time.stopwatch_start(&watch)
>        //One of the two below repeated 25 times
>        gdAPI.Packed_Array_Utils.ArrayRef(r_return, &ret)
>        //Destroy(r_return)
>        //GDW.Array_M_List.Create1(r_return, {&ret})
>        time.stopwatch_stop(&watch)
>    ```

1. You reuse the same array. After the first run, the reference will already be assigned and no work needs to be done anymore. This doesn't reflect a real use case.
1. You compare only `array_ref` vs. a full `destroy` + `create` cycle. Of course that's much faster, but it's not expressive because you're not doing isolated `array_ref` calls in reality, you combine them with another FFI call.

TLDR: you'd need to measure two end-to-end scenarios that _do the same thing_ (e.g. fetch and assign an array).
It's also important because this will tell us how many % the `array_ref` approach gains over an alternative.

Btw, you can use \`\`\`odin tags for syntax highlighting :slightly_smiling_face:

Thanks for the feedback! I even mentioned the early return in the conclusion 🤦 
I did the 25x repetition because the array_ref was too fast to capture on the stopwatch some frames. I could prep 25 different arrays and pass those through the two different methods so that it's different arrays each time.

> You compare only array_ref vs. a full destroy + create cycle. Of course that's much faster, but it's not expressive because you're not doing isolated array_ref calls in reality, you combine them with another FFI call.

Only using Create1 causes a mem leak when the destination array is already initialized. What does godot-cpp and rust do differently? I do want to get this comparison right.

@dsnopek Any chance that we can get this merged? No one has provided an alternative to the destructor + constructor1 pattern for a = operation. This pattern is used by godot-cpp. By @Bromeon 's own admission > You compare only array_ref vs. a full destroy + create cycle. Of course that's much faster It seems to be a common sense difference in speed. Utilization of array_ref and dictionary_ref will allow for an optimization to godot-cpp's = operators. This could be expanded to the other ref counted types for a similar improvement, as they all follow the destructor + constructor1 pattern :) [edit for typo]

> By @Bromeon 's own admission
> 
> > You compare only array_ref vs. a full destroy + create cycle. Of course that's much faster
> 
> It seems to be a common sense difference in speed.

There's a misunderstanding, my comment meant we're comparing apples with oranges.

I implemented this operation [in Rust](https://github.com/godot-rust/gdext/blob/107a87e3cb0d6bc7f4685907524682c8d9ce544e/godot-ffi/src/godot_ffi.rs#L218-L220), without `array_ref` **and** without full destroy + create. It uses pointer-swap.
Now I'm not sure if the same is possible in C++ since `operator=` is a bit more involved. But it should be explored.

---

> Utilization of array_ref and dictionary_ref will allow for an optimization to godot-cpp's = operators.
> 
> This could be expanded to the other ref counted types for a similar improvement, as they all follow the destructor + constructor1 pattern :)

This is actually a good reason _not_ to provide `array_ref`, because the pattern would need to be repeated for every single type with custom ctor/dtor. If we really need to follow this route, it would be better to provide a generic API, like we do for constructors and destructors:
```c
GDExtensionPtrAssigner variant_get_ptr_assigner(GDExtensionVariantType type);
```
But again, we should absolutely make sure this is 100% needed, as it's only an optimization but comes with quite a bit of complexity. Does Odin share C++'s (rather annoying) copy semantics with `operator=`? :slightly_smiling_face:

> Does Odin share C++'s (rather annoying) copy semantics with operator=? 🙂

Not using the pattern is unavoidable in certain cases and unsafe otherwise.

If the destination array is already initialized the constructor1 does not validate that it is or isn't initialized. There would need to be additional tracking on the state of the destination to determine if it needs to be destroyed or not. If the destination arrayType is already initialized this causes a memory leak because the reference was dropped without dereferencing it.

It is unavoidable when returning an array in a function call from Godot. ie a getter of an array. Godot provides an already initialized array in the return pointer because it must initialize a variant for r_ret before making the function call. How does Rust handle this situation?

`GDExtensionPtrAssigner `
This would be confusing as the ptr getter does not mess with the refcount and was made to get a pointer from a variant. There are no variants involved in the process that requires destruction+constructor.
The issue that array_ref solves is specifically around verifying if the destination variable is holding an initialized array, dereferencing the array in the destination variable, refcounting the original array and then assigning it to the destination variable. All in a single GDE call.

> because the pattern would need to be repeated for every single type with custom ctor/dtor. If we really need to follow this route, it would be better to provide a generic API, like we do for constructors and destructors

Yes. It's odd that the = operator isn't exposed as a builtin alongside the other operator overloads. (==, !=, >, <,  etc.) It would be very nice if we could get those directly.

> It is unavoidable when returning an array in a function call from Godot. ie a getter of an array. Godot provides an already initialized array in the return pointer because it must initialize a variant for r_ret before making the function call. How does Rust handle this situation?

I linked it above; we do a swap between the already-initialized dest and the to-be-returned value.

---

> Not using the pattern is unavoidable in certain cases and unsafe otherwise.

Is it? `operator=` can almost always be implemented via copy-constructor + swap. C++ even has [a widespread idiom](https://stackoverflow.com/q/3279543) for it.
I really think the only reason to deviate is possibly performance, not inevitability or unsafety.

---

> Yes. It's odd that the = operator isn't exposed as a builtin alongside the other operator overloads. (==, !=, >, <, etc.) It would be very nice if we could get those directly.

Keep in mind that GDExtension is a C API, not a C++ one. Its purpose is to provide the common denominator for all binding languages, not 1:1 map C++.

Further, `operator=` is an idiosyncrasy unique to C++. Most languages either have reference semantics (GC/refcount) or _sane_ value semantics (Rust with moves). The whole ceremony around `operator=` and its pitfalls is a non-issue for most :wink:

> we do a swap between the already-initialized dest and the to-be-returned value.

When does that already-initialized dest get dereferenced and what do you call to decrement its refcount (destroy). A swap as I would understand it moves it from one variable to the other unless there's additional things happening due to the "swap" call itself.

// RAII will destroy (now empty) result -> cheap.

I assume that result now stores out_slot? By what means does it destroy result?

> I assume that result now stores out_slot?

Yes, they were swapped.

> By what means does it destroy result?

Just calling its destructor using the corresponding C function, like everytime you need to destroy something. Are you familiar with this part of the GDExtension API?

I wrote the entirety of Toxin on my own. It outperforms the C++ implementation of GDE. Of course I know that. But you're not saying plainly what is going on behind the scenes of your swap function.

Does it increment the ref count of the original array?
Does the C destructor get called? yes now you said it plainly.
Are you magically avoiding one or the other?

Because as far as I'm aware there is a need for both or GDScript's scope will decrement the original array when the scope exits and now it's at -1 from where it should be.

> I wrote the entirety of Toxin on my own. It outperforms the C++ implementation of GDE. Of course I know that.

I wasn't questioning your authority. It was a genuine question, I'm happy to explain how I implemented things :slightly_smiling_face: 

---

> But you're not saying plainly what is going on behind the scenes of your swap function.

Again, I linked the code, you'll see that it's not my swap function but `std::ptr::swap` from the Rust standard library :wink:

It doesn't do anything besides bitwise copies. The destructor is called _outside_ the swap -- but that's nothing special, it's just a value (array in this case) falling out of scope and RAII kicking in.

My pseudocode above covers all the inc-refs/dec-refs needed. In the case of returning a value, IIRC 1 dec-ref (destructor) and 0 inc-refs are involved (no copies).

Could you maybe check if this pattern would also be applicable in Odin? :thinking:

My testing had shown that it needs an inc-ref on the source array. If godot-cpp is using the operator= to return values they are doing the same. 

I don't know rust or how it was decided to implement things in rust, so I'm reliant in you to help fill in the blanks. Like the fact that there is a destructor called automatically (not certain which one) when something goes out of scope. 

Does rust automatically handle any ref counting when passing ref counted types to other functions?

> @dsnopek Any chance that we can get this merged? No one has provided an alternative to the destructor + constructor1 pattern for a = operation. This pattern is used by godot-cpp.

I don't think the right profiling has been done here yet.

A better test would be taking godot-cpp and calling an actual Godot function that returns `Array` and comparing the performance with the current implementation versus one taking advantage of `array_ref`.

From the code, we can see that using `array_ref` would avoid one allocation/deallocation (that of the `Array` itself) but not the internal `ArrayPrivate`. The question is if that even matters. It might not!

When Godot is calling GDExtension methods, the `Array` return value is allocated on the stack, and the `ArrayPrivate` on the heap. Is avoiding that allocation on the stack meaningful?
